reading.rtitle: What the Average Did Not Say
paras: Two years ago a credit team in Porto Alegre put one number on the first slide of every review: the average limit. It was eight hundred reais, and for a while nobody asked anything else. The number was easy to say and easy to remember, and that was the whole problem.

The team was not careless. They checked the average every month, and it hardly moved. What they did not check was the range. Most of the customers were far below eight hundred, on limits of three or four hundred, and a few hundred people sat far above it, on limits of five thousand. Hardly anybody was near the average at all.

In the second quarter the losses rose, and the average still did not move. It took two months to see why. Almost all of the new losses came from the small group at the top of the range, and that group was a tiny share of the customers and most of the money. The average was hiding them the whole time, because a number that describes everybody describes nobody.

They did not throw the average away. They put two more numbers next to it: the range, and the share of the portfolio held by the largest one per cent of limits. The three lines together take five seconds longer to read, and the surprises stopped.
reading.source: A composite account of a Brazilian credit desk, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a credit team calculates an average.
To show how one number on a slide hid the real risk, and what the team put next to it.
To argue that averages should never be used in a business review.

items.situation: Say the default rate and the baseline out loud, and give the gap.
tips: Four point two per cent, against a baseline of three point one, so the gap is one point one.
Point, never comma. Four comma two does not exist in English.

items.situation: Say how much of the base is in the pilot, without giving an exact number.
tips: Roughly a third of the base is in the pilot.
About, around and roughly all work here.

items.situation: Now use a quantifier with something you cannot count.
tips: We do not have much data on that cohort yet.
In a positive sentence, say a lot of data, not much data.

items.situation: Say what the average limit hides, in one sentence.
tips: Hardly any customer sits at the average; the range goes from three hundred to five thousand.
Hardly any works with countable nouns and means almost none.

items.situation: Read two real figures from your own dashboard out loud, with a comparison for each.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about an average I just showed you.

listenings.text: Let me take you through the page. The default rate is four point two per cent this quarter, against a baseline of three point one, so we are one point one above where we started and zero point two above target. Roughly a third of the base is now in the pilot, and the sample is finally big enough to trust. Two months ago it was not, and I said so at the time. The average limit is eight hundred reais. I am going to say that number once, and then I am going to ask you to forget it, because hardly any customer sits at eight hundred. The range goes from three hundred to five thousand, and the range is where the story is. Revenue exceeded the target by eleven per cent, and most of the losses come from the customers who joined in April.

In the nineteen forties the American air force had a problem with crashes, and for a while they blamed the pilots. Then somebody measured four thousand of them: height, arm length, chest, ten measurements in all. The cockpit was designed for the average pilot, so the question was simple. How many of the four thousand were average on all ten? The answer was none. Not a small number. None. And on just three of the ten, fewer than four in a hundred. That is what an average always does. It hides the range, and the two ends of the range are where the interesting cases live. So whenever somebody shows you an average, ask two things. How many people are actually near it, and what do the two ends look like? If nobody can answer, the number is decoration.
